intro: William Meath Baker, squire of Hasfield, gets the shortest of Elgar’s portraits. His brisk announcements become hard accents; his hurried exit supplies the punchline.

sections.label: Var 4 · Baker bangs the door
sections.mNote: Repeated accents and a bustling Allegro di molto

cues.title: Baker takes the floor
cues.text: Strings and woodwinds speak in clipped, heavily accented phrases, with horns, trumpets and timpani behind them. The marking is Allegro di molto. Almost before this bustling little speech has begun, the orchestra is racing towards its last chord.
cues.evidence: Novello full score, pp. 20–23, rehearsal figures 11–14: opening accents and the concise ending. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/1e/IMSLP23792-PMLP07276-Elgar_-_Enigma_Variations_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Carriages for the guests
cues.text: Baker has a houseful of guests and carriages to arrange. With a slip of paper in his hand, he reads out the day’s plans forcefully and hurries from the music room, accidentally banging the door. Elgar includes the guests’ teasing response in the middle of the variation.
cues.evidence: Elgar, My Friends Pictured Within (Novello), section IV: the paper, carriage arrangements, door and guests’ response in bars 15–24. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/06/IMSLP339677-SIBLEY1802.27173.6d2a-39087004945996text.pdf. Baker’s Hasfield home: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_Variations

source.title: Elgar, Enigma Variations, full score (Novello)
source.locator: Novello full score, pp. 20–23, rehearsal figures 11–14: Variation IV, W.M.B., marked Allegro di molto.

timeline.note: Strings and woodwinds begin with clipped accents, reinforced by horns, trumpets and timpani (p. 20).
First violins, violas, cellos and basses run beneath the longer wind notes. Flutes and low brass join the exchange (pp. 20–21).
Oboes and clarinets chatter in short notes. Flute and violin flourishes interrupt them while the other strings leave gaps (p. 22).
The full orchestra returns to the opening accents, now marked fff, and ends with a sudden stop (pp. 22–23).

composer.epithet: He made the Enigma Variations from his friendships and preserved his own way with the music on gramophone records.
facts: His father’s Worcester music shop; violin and organ; composition largely self-taught
Powick bandmaster, instrumental teacher and organist at St George’s, Worcester
Two symphonies; violin and cello concertos; Gerontius; five Pomp and Circumstance marches
Master of the King’s Musick from 1924; recordings of his own orchestral works
composer.background:
Elgar grew up among the instruments and sheet music in his father’s Worcester shop. William tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church; Edward studied the scores, learned several instruments and earned money with his violin. Born at Lower Broadheath on 2 June 1857, he had hoped to study at Leipzig, but the family could not afford it. His education continued in rehearsal rooms. Playing in the Three Choirs Festival orchestra, he learned the choral music of Handel and Mendelssohn from inside the string section.

From 1879 to 1884 he was bandmaster at Worcester County Asylum, Powick. He trained members of staff to play for the patients and supplied quadrilles and polkas for the Friday-evening dances. Here was an orchestra whose players he knew individually, with capabilities he had to accommodate. His other work included teaching in local schools and giving private lessons in Malvern. In 1885 he succeeded William at the organ of St George’s.
